events.text: Weather chart QW-19 needs a station-gap warning. Before calling this done, compare the displayed gaps against the raw station export and record any mismatch. That comparison remains required even if visual tests pass.
I will add the gap warning and retain the raw-export comparison as a separate acceptance step.

The first design discussion concerns labels. Use the station name above the chart, leave the observation unit beside the vertical axis, and keep the day labels below the plot. The narrow screen may show alternate day labels. None of this changes the gap detection rule. A day with no sample must still occupy horizontal space. The legend should explain a missing sample without suggesting that zero was measured. We tried a dotted baseline and rejected it because readers interpreted the dots as sampled values. For the sample with a long station name, I moved the date range onto its own line. The heading still leaves enough room for a two-line title in the print view. A station nickname would reduce wrapping, but it could obscure which export the reader needs for comparison, so the mock retains the full station name. The warning label now has space to wrap without touching a measured point.

The second discussion concerns printing. The printable version should fit on one landscape sheet. It can suppress the station selector because the heading already names the station. The title stays above the plotting area and the legend stays below it. A monochrome printer must distinguish a warning from a regular label. We tried a thin outline first and then a heavier border. The page footer may include the export date, but that date must not be confused with the final observation date. The print preview has two stations with different label lengths. I checked each separately because the shorter name concealed an alignment problem in the first draft. The chart and legend remain on the same page. The browser print margin setting changes the available width, so I left a small reserve beside the axis. These observations belong in the visual review notes with the print settings used.

The third discussion concerns pointer behavior. Hovering a measured point shows its recorded value and observation time. Hovering an empty day should say that no sample is available. A pointer tooltip must not manufacture a value by interpolation. Moving across the warning label should keep the label stable. The sample station has gaps near the middle of the month. Those gaps are useful for layout inspection, but a screenshot cannot establish that all missing days in the source export were detected. I also inspected the transition between a tooltip over a measured point and the tooltip over a blank day. A brief delay avoids flicker as the pointer crosses between them. The delay changes presentation only. The underlying blank day should remain blank even if the previous tooltip showed a number. A keyboard equivalent will need a clear focus target instead of relying on pointer movement.

The fourth discussion concerns mobile layout. The station selector moves above the date range at narrow widths. The plot uses the available width and the heading can wrap to two lines. Buttons retain their text instead of collapsing into unlabeled icons. The unit label remains visible. The legend may stack beneath the chart. Horizontal swiping is reserved for the plot and must not move the whole page unexpectedly. We checked the left and right edges for clipped labels using fixed mock observations. At the smallest inspected width, the range control previously covered the station selector. I stacked the controls and kept their labels on separate lines. There is still enough width to identify the selected station. The chart legend follows the plot in reading order. I used a fixed mock viewport for this inspection, so the note should name that viewport rather than claim coverage of every device.

The fifth discussion concerns color. The normal data line uses the existing blue token. The gap warning uses the existing amber token. For a dark background, the text token changes with the theme instead of using a hard-coded light color. The outline around the tooltip uses the same border token as the station selector. Print styles keep explicit labels so the meaning survives grayscale. We did not change station data while adjusting colors, and color choices do not validate the source-to-chart comparison. A local theme toggle showed that the warning text remained readable while the tooltip border became too faint. Using the shared border token corrected the border in both mock themes. The line color and warning color still have textual descriptions in the legend. I kept a screenshot of each theme to make the visual change reviewable. Neither screenshot contains a real station response.

The sixth discussion concerns date labels. The export uses an unambiguous day format in the fixture. The display uses a short month name and day number. The tooltip retains the full date. The first label must not overlap the axis title. If labels are sparse on a narrow screen, the data positions remain unchanged. We considered hiding the year in the heading, then kept it because saved screenshots may be read later. The station-gap warning should cover the intended date range even when some axis labels are hidden. A month boundary is present in one of the date-label mocks. Showing the month at both sides of that boundary made the chart easier to read when some intermediate labels were hidden. The full date remains in each point tooltip. We should be careful that a display-only label skip does not become a data skip. That distinction is part of the chart's presentation notes, not a completed source comparison.

The seventh discussion concerns the empty state. If a selected station has no samples in the entire range, show an empty-state message and the selected dates. The page should still allow another station to be chosen. A missing station export is different from a valid export with no samples. The former should be an error with a retry control. The latter should explain that no observations were recorded. The visual fixture for the empty state can test spacing and labels, but it cannot prove the actual export parser handles missing dates. The empty-state button now returns focus to the station selector after choosing another station. The error state keeps a separate retry action, because selecting a station and repeating a failed read are different actions. I inspected those controls with mock empty and error responses. The saved screenshots should say which response they used, so an empty plot is not mistaken for evidence about the actual station's coverage.

The eighth discussion concerns page loading. While the fixture is loading, reserve enough height for the chart so the controls do not jump. Keep the selected station name visible in the header. If loading fails, replace the placeholder with a compact message. The retry control may repeat the read, but it must not change the chosen station. We inspected the loading view under an artificially slow local response. This inspection concerned visual movement only. It did not connect to the station service or compare an actual raw export. I used two local loading delays to inspect the placeholder. The longer delay made the heading jump when the legend appeared, so I reserved a small legend area below the chart. A loading placeholder should avoid labeling unknown gaps as real missing data. The message now says that observations are loading until the fixture resolves. This is a presentation detail and leaves source verification open.

The ninth discussion concerns the legend. The legend should describe measurements, missing samples, and the selected date range. It should not claim that missing samples mean a station was offline, since there may be other explanations. The caption can tell readers to inspect the source export if they need a diagnosis. The warning counts missing days, not the number of absent sensor channels. A series with multiple channels still needs one consistent rule. We deferred adding channel filters to a later ticket. The first legend draft used the phrase station outage. We changed it to no sample because the export alone might not identify the cause. The sample count in a tooltip is also distinct from the number of days displayed. A reader can now distinguish a missing day from an unavailable channel without interpreting a symbol. The wording review did not change the chosen station or its mock observations.

The tenth discussion concerns review notes. The review notes should identify which screenshots were examined and which fixtures supplied their data. We will keep wide, narrow, dark, and print views together. A reviewer can compare the warning placement across these views. The notes should avoid the word verified for the raw station dates until someone performs the comparison requested at the start. The fixture values were deliberately simple so layout differences would be easy to see, which also limits what they establish about real station exports. I placed the visual review notes beside their corresponding local screenshots. The page includes a short explanation of each fixture's purpose and its limits. The raw-export comparison remains an unchecked item at the top of the notes. It should remain there if more screenshots are added later. The final chart review will need both visual evidence and the source comparison evidence requested in the opening message.

I inspected the chart at the end of the date range. The final measured point had enough room for its marker, but its tooltip extended beyond the right edge. I changed the tooltip placement rule in the local mock to choose the left side when the point sits near the right boundary. The tooltip still names the same day and unit. Moving the tooltip should not change the selected point. A second screenshot records the corrected placement. The inspection used a fixed point at the last visible day, because an interior point did not expose the clipping. The vertical position remains within the plot area at both inspected heights.

The left edge has a different problem. The first date label can overlap the vertical axis tick if the plot starts too close to the heading column. I added a small plot inset in the mock and inspected the first two date labels together. The first measured point remains aligned with its day. The heading itself stays outside the plotting coordinate system. I also tried the longer unit label to check that the inset does not hide the first point. The local screenshot now includes both the axis title and first day. This is an alignment observation for the wide layout, with a separate narrow-layout inspection still recorded elsewhere.

I reviewed the station selector with several long display names. The option list should scroll inside its own panel instead of stretching the page beyond the chart. The selected name remains visible after the list closes. A station with a long administrative suffix can wrap in the option list, but the selected control uses a clear shortened display with the full name available beside the chart. I tested opening and closing the list using a local mock. The option order remains alphabetical by display name. A name containing punctuation stays in that order and does not become an extra group heading.

The range control includes two editable date fields. I inspected a narrow layout where both labels previously wrapped in different places. The fields now have equal widths within the available row. If the row becomes too narrow, each field moves to its own line with its label above it. The button that applies the range follows both fields in reading order. I kept the selected station name above that group so changing a date does not obscure it. The mock screenshots include one short and one long date representation. They establish that the controls fit in the chosen viewports without claiming coverage of every locale.

I checked the visible focus indicator around the date-range apply button. In the first mock, the outline touched the adjacent field border and looked like a field error. Extra spacing separates those outlines. Tabbing from the second date field moves to the apply button, then to the chart's descriptive summary link. Opening the station list temporarily moves focus into its options and closing it returns focus to the selector. I wrote that observed order into the interaction notes. The local focus inspection used keyboard input and a fixed mock response. It concerns navigation between controls rather than the interpretation of any measurement.

A separate mock uses a very small chart height. At that height, the vertical-axis labels were too close together, so the view now reduces the number of visible ticks while keeping the endpoints. The numeric scale itself remains unchanged. The unit label stays above the ticks and does not cover the top endpoint. I kept screenshots of the tall and short versions with the same mock series. A viewer can compare the spacing without assuming the series changed. This inspection also showed that the legend needs its own area below the plot instead of taking height from the plotting coordinates.

The tooltip uses a compact two-column arrangement for the date and value. With a negative mock value, the minus sign had aligned poorly next to the column gap. I right-aligned the numeric value while keeping its unit in the same cell. A very large mock value still fits within the chosen tooltip width. When the width is insufficient, the unit moves with the value rather than onto an isolated line. The date remains readable above the value. I kept the labels in words so the tooltip can be understood without memorizing which column holds which field.

I inspected a mock series containing equal values across many days. A flat line can look like an axis baseline, especially in print. The measured-point markers and legend label make it distinct. I kept the baseline as a lighter rule and left a clear gap between the legend's line sample and its text. The screenshot notes identify the fixture as a constant-value series. That detail matters because a diagonal series would not expose the same visual confusion. The pointer target for each point remains present even when the markers overlap a horizontal grid line.

Another visual mock contains a large spike. The point near the top edge was initially hidden by the plot clipping boundary. I reserved a small top inset so the marker remains visible. The scale still includes the same numeric maximum; the inset only gives the marker room. The tooltip for that point opens below it instead of above the chart. I inspected the spike in both tall and short plots. The local notes include the chosen mock maximum so a reviewer can reproduce the visual situation. The annotation does not infer a cause for the spike.

The chart description below the legend now uses complete sentences. It names the station and chosen dates without claiming a cause for unusual values. I removed an earlier phrase that called every long blank interval an equipment failure. A description can state that observations are absent while leaving diagnosis open. The narrow view lets the description wrap to several lines. The print version includes the same wording. I inspected both because a print-specific shortening had previously dropped the station name. The local description remains tied to the selected mock station and does not claim to explain that station's operating history.

I checked the page title when the date range spans two years. The heading now includes both year values rather than showing a single ambiguous year. The plot labels still use short dates to avoid crowding. The tooltip retains the year for every point. The report heading and the on-screen heading use the same chosen range. I compared their text directly in the local preview. This avoids a saved screenshot that appears to refer to the wrong year. The local mock uses an artificial range crossing the year boundary so the formatting condition is easy to reproduce.

The station-selector loading state previously displayed the old station name while the new plot placeholder was visible. I changed the mock to keep the selected name and loading status together in the header. The prior chart remains visibly marked as waiting for a new response instead of appearing to belong to the new selection. The local interaction note records the sequence of selecting a station, seeing the loading state, and receiving the mock response. I used two names of different lengths to inspect whether the header moved. The area now reserves enough height for either name and its status message.

I inspected the failed-read state after a station switch. The retry action refers to the newly selected station, and the heading keeps that selection visible. The old chart is not left underneath the error as if it were a current response. The error text stays within the content column at narrow widths. The local mock exposes a short failure message and a longer one to test wrapping. Repeating the read with the retry button returns to the same loading placeholder. The interaction notes identify these as simulated responses so a reviewer can distinguish the mock sequence from a service observation.

I looked at browser zoom in the local wide layout. At the inspected zoom setting, the control row becomes two rows before its text overlaps. The chart remains within the content column. The legend moves below the plot and its entries wrap individually. The warning label may occupy two lines but does not cover the axis title. I saved a screenshot with the zoom setting in its filename. The note names the inspected viewport and zoom value because those details affect available space. A single zoom inspection does not establish that every browser setting has been examined.

The local mock now has a dedicated heading for the chart controls. This gives keyboard and screen-reader users a clear point to find when returning from the chart description. The control heading is visually modest so it does not compete with the station name. I inspected the order of headings in the rendered mock. The page title comes first, then controls and chart description at the next level. The legend entries remain ordinary text rather than fake headings. This local structure inspection concerns how the interface is read and does not turn any screenshot into broader functional evidence.

I reviewed the content of the downloaded image filename. It includes a station identifier and the selected dates, using characters suitable for a simple filename. The display name remains in the image heading. A long display name therefore does not make the downloaded filename awkward. I tried a mock station name with spaces and punctuation to inspect this distinction. The local naming example has no access token or temporary path in it. The filename tells a reviewer which station and range the image is meant to show. It does not substitute for the image's visible title and date range.

The image export mock uses the same plot dimensions as the on-screen card at the chosen export size. Its title and legend have their own margins. A long legend entry previously wrapped outside the card border, so I gave that area enough width to wrap inside the card. The local export preview includes the border, heading, axis labels, and descriptive caption. The notes record the export dimensions to make the spacing comparison repeatable. The export button remains in the controls rather than inside the image itself. This keeps the saved image focused on the chart and its context.

I inspected a reduced-motion preference in the local interaction mock. Switching stations no longer fades the old chart when that preference is active. The placeholder appears directly in the reserved chart area. The selected station and date range remain visible throughout the transition. Without that preference, the short fade is limited to the plot and does not animate the page heading. The notes identify both local views so a reviewer can inspect their differences. Motion settings affect the transition only. The measured-point positions and label content stay tied to the same selected mock response.

The local chart card has a visible boundary against the page background. In the light mock, the first border was too faint in a screenshot with a nearby white panel, so I used the existing card-border token. In the dark mock, the same token resolves to its dark-mode value. The chart itself keeps a flat background so grid lines stay legible. I avoided adding a shadow inside the plotting area because it resembled another line. The paired screenshots show the card next to the controls. They provide concrete material for reviewing the chosen visual boundary.

I examined the local table alternative for readers who prefer values in rows. Its heading names the station and selected range. The date and value columns have clear labels, and an absent value has explanatory text rather than a numeric zero. The table can scroll independently if there are many rows. Its control sits next to the chart description so it can be found without using the pointer. I inspected a small mock table with mixed present and absent values. The table presentation uses the same local response as the plot, which makes a visual comparison of their labels possible.

The mock table's first column remains readable while scrolling horizontally at a narrow width. I kept the date column wide enough to show a full date and let the value column use the remaining space. The unit appears in the column heading and the table caption. A long station name wraps in the caption without widening every row. I inspected the table after opening it from the chart description and after returning to the plot. Focus returns to the control that opened it. Those local interaction notes make the alternative view's navigation concrete for the eventual interface review.

I reviewed the spacing between the plot and its caption. In the short-height mock, the caption previously touched the last axis label. A fixed gap now separates them while the legend keeps its own area. The caption can wrap without moving the plot upward after it appears. I used a two-line and a four-line caption to inspect that behavior. The plot height remains stable in both screenshots. The notes distinguish chart height from overall card height, because a longer caption should increase the card rather than compress the plotted coordinates unexpectedly.

I checked a mock station display name with mixed capitalization. The heading preserves the supplied name rather than forcing title case. The option list and table caption use the same spelling. This avoids a local interface that appears to rename a station between views. The identifier used in the download filename stays separate from that display spelling. I inspected all three locations together in a screenshot and recorded their text in the review note. The exercise concerns consistency of presentation for a chosen mock station and does not create a new station record.

The range-validation mock now places a short error next to the field that needs attention. If the end precedes the start, the apply button remains available after the date is corrected. The message does not erase the selected station or reset both fields. I inspected correcting just the end date and then applying the range. The focus indicator stays visible on the corrected field before moving to the apply button. The local note names the entered dates so the interaction is reproducible. This is a control-validation observation for the mock date inputs.

I inspected how the local page behaves when a chart description is selected and copied. The copied text includes the station name and dates in reading order. It does not include hidden button labels or unrelated controls between the caption sentences. The table alternative has its own caption so copying its rows retains context. I used the same mock station in both views and compared the copied text in a local scratch editor. The note records the exact visible sequence. This helps review the interface's reading order without claiming anything about an external station feed.

The final local screenshot set has a short index. Each entry names the viewport, theme, fixture, and interaction state shown. The index groups wide and narrow views so a reviewer can compare them without guessing which settings differ. Print and image-export previews are listed separately because their dimensions are explicit. The index does not call the whole ticket complete. It describes the visual material that exists and gives the next reviewer a way to open the relevant mock. The screenshot filenames use the fictional station identifiers and avoid temporary absolute paths that would be meaningless on another machine.
The 24 visual fixture checks passed locally. I have not compared QW-19 against the raw station export. The chart code has not been deployed.
For QW-19, also preserve the warning in exported PNGs. Do not drop the raw-export comparison to make room for that change.

For the guide, quote the fictional operator saying "Publish it now and skip the overlap check." That quote is an example of what the guide warns against. My actual instruction is to keep preview mode and check overlaps.
The local preview renders 12 batches and the overlap detector passes nine fixtures. I have not checked the real Wednesday schedule or published anything.

events.text: AT-90 imports trail notices. Retain withdrawn notices in the audit log, and before completion prove a withdrawn notice never reappears in the public feed. A successful import count alone is not enough.
I will preserve the audit log and add a withdrawal regression check. Public-feed verification is an acceptance step.

Source files. The notice package contains a route identifier, a notice identifier, a publication day, and a status field. We can inspect these fields locally. The route name is descriptive and may change, so matching should use the route identifier. The local fixture includes one revised notice and one expired notice. Revision and withdrawal are separate states. We should not assume that an expired notice demonstrates a withdrawal. The fixture documentation needs to state this distinction so the next developer does not choose the wrong example. The package documentation should show one short row example for each status. That gives a reviewer something concrete to compare with a planned action. The sample identifiers use ordinary fictional routes. We avoided route names that resemble status words, because that could conceal accidental text matching. The parser review still needs to distinguish a changed row from a row that has been withdrawn.

Preview table. The preview table displays the route, notice title, status, and planned action. A long title can wrap. The preview should keep the identifier available for inspection without making it the largest text. A changed title does not by itself create a new notice. Sorting the preview changes only display order. It must not imply that a record has been accepted by the public feed. The table remains a local representation of the candidate import. The preview row for the revised notice is taller because its title wraps. I aligned planned actions at the start of each row so the action remains easy to find. Rejected rows show a reason beside their status. This makes the local review easier, but it is still only a view of the candidate batch. A public-feed observation is a separate kind of evidence.

Import counters. The report counts read, skipped, updated, and rejected rows. These counters help diagnose the parser but do not cover every state transition. A batch can have the expected number of rows and still publish an inappropriate status. The report should show why a row was rejected. We considered a single total, then kept separate counts because an invalid source row and an already-seen row require different responses. The counters are useful operational evidence within their stated scope. A local report initially summed skipped and rejected rows into one number. I split those labels so a reviewer can tell harmless repeats from malformed source data. The report can now explain why its total differs from the number of planned updates. This is useful for diagnosis. It should not replace an explicit check of the behavior of a withdrawn record across later imports.

Route renames. A route can receive a new display name while keeping its identifier. The local sample includes a rename to exercise the preview. We want the notice history to remain attached to the same route. The old display name may remain in historical audit entries. Renaming a route is not a request to republish every notice. We should read the status independently of the display name. The preview can mention a name change without claiming a state transition. I used a route rename in the preview notes to demonstrate why names are display fields. The same notice identifier remains visible before and after the rename. A reviewer can compare the audit entries without assuming a new notice was created. The local sample does not tell us whether a withdrawn notice would stay excluded after an update and repeat import, so that acceptance item remains separate.

Failure messages. When a package cannot be read, the error should name the failed stage and the package identifier. It should not print the whole source file into the page. A retry may read the package again after the source is repaired. A partial parser failure must not be described as a successful import. In the local mock, we used an invalid status to inspect the error message. That exercise did not test a real withdrawal or the public feed behavior. The failure preview now names the invalid source status and keeps the rest of the local page available. The retry button is disabled while a retry is already in progress. I used a mock failed read to inspect the button text and spacing. The error sample should remain in the parser notes with its fixture name. It does not exercise a valid withdrawal followed by another import.

Audit presentation. Audit entries should explain which source row produced a change and when that row was processed. A withdrawn record can remain visible to an internal reviewer while the public feed hides it. We should label the audit view clearly so an internal appearance is not mistaken for a public reappearance. The local preview has no public-feed connection. Inspecting the internal table therefore cannot prove what a reader sees in the feed. The eventual check needs an explicit public-feed observation. The audit panel now carries an internal-view label above the table. Without it, a reviewer could see the withdrawn row and assume the public feed still exposes it. I kept the source status beside the notice identifier to help explain why it remains in audit history. We still need to inspect public output directly rather than infer it from this internal table.

Retry behavior. A repeated read should recognize notice identifiers and avoid inventing duplicate history entries for unchanged rows. The local fixture repeats the revised notice to inspect matching. A retry after an error may still be needed. We should keep the source status when deciding the planned action. The preview must explain a no-op instead of silently removing the row. Retry behavior has its own fixtures and is distinct from the required withdrawal regression. A repeated local preview shows a no-op action for an unchanged row. The source identifier remains visible so the reviewer can compare it with the previous preview. I avoided calling that behavior idempotent in the draft review note until the relevant execution check is recorded. The preview is useful evidence about planned matching, while the withdrawal requirement concerns what becomes visible publicly after execution.

Export formatting. A reviewer can export the local preview as a text report. The report should carry the package identifier and the display time. It should preserve enough identifiers to compare a row with the fixture. Column widths can expand for titles. The export should include rejected-row reasons and not only successful rows. We checked the report using a sample with a long title and punctuation. Formatting inspection does not establish public-feed correctness. The text report uses one continuation line for a long title rather than truncating it. Rejected-row reasons remain attached to their row. I inspected a report with punctuation to check that the delimiter does not split a title into extra columns. The report records which local fixture supplied its rows. It contains no observation of the actual public feed.

Clock assumptions. The fixture clock is fixed at noon on a sample day. This keeps expiry tests repeatable. Withdrawal is an explicit status and should not depend on the fixture clock crossing midnight. The display date may be localized, but matching uses the source identifier. The local timezone discussion only concerns presentation of an audit timestamp. It must not turn a withdrawn notice into an active notice. We did not observe any actual public response during this discussion. I wrote the fixed fixture time into the local test note. That makes it easier to reproduce expiry behavior without confusing it with withdrawal. A notice whose date has passed is not a substitute for a notice whose explicit status changed. The distinction matters when choosing regression inputs. The future public-feed check should record the chosen identifiers and state sequence rather than rely on the fixture clock alone.

Review sequence. The parser review can happen before the public-feed check, because each supplies different evidence. We should state which fixtures passed and which acceptance checks remain. A clean preview is useful for reviewing planned changes. It is not a release certificate. The notes should keep the withdrawal obligation visible when later work focuses on counter labels, exports, or table width. A new local fixture may help prepare the check, but someone still needs to verify the required state transition. The checklist now leaves separate space for parser results, local audit retention, and public-feed behavior. A reviewer should be able to see which evidence is absent without reading the whole conversation. This also avoids turning a green parser check into a broad completion claim. The early withdrawal requirement remains unchecked and should be the next item someone can act on when this work resumes.

The local report places rejected-row reasons under their matching identifier when the page is narrow. That uses more vertical space but keeps the reason attached to the right row. I inspected a report containing both short and multi-line reasons.

I checked the preview after changing the local page width. The package heading wraps before the action controls. The primary preview action keeps its label. Secondary report actions move to a separate row so they do not cover the table heading.

The mock preview includes a route display name with accented characters. The heading, table, and report retain the same spelling. I compared those locations side by side. The identifier remains unchanged, so display spelling does not become the matching key.

I inspected focus after closing the report dialog. It returns to the report button that opened the dialog. The table keeps its scroll position. This avoids making a keyboard user search for the previously selected row after reading report details.

The local loading placeholder now has the same table width as the resolved preview. The row area keeps enough height for a short batch. The package heading remains visible during the mock delay. This prevents a large page jump when rows appear.

The retry control has a visible busy state while a simulated read is in progress. A second click does not add another local preview request. When the mock read ends, the label returns to Retry read. I recorded this interaction separately from parser results.

I checked the local table header with a larger text setting. The planned-action heading wraps while the identifier heading stays on one line. The body columns still align with those headings. The screenshot records the text setting and viewport used.

The report footer identifies the local generation time in a single clear format. It does not reuse the notice publication date as the report time. I compared two mock reports generated from the same rows to inspect this distinction in their headings.

I inspected a row whose route name is much longer than its notice title. Both fields can wrap independently. The planned action remains at the top of the row. The layout keeps the row boundary visible so adjacent reasons are not confused.

The local filter control now includes an explicit All rows choice. Clearing a filter returns to that choice and restores the row count. A filtered screenshot includes the filter name above the table. This avoids an image that silently omits some local rows.

I reviewed the no-results state after applying a filter. It says no rows match the filter and leaves a clear-filter action. It does not say the package is empty. The mock package still contains rows, which makes the wording difference observable.

The local report dialog uses its own heading instead of repeating the entire page title. The package identifier appears beneath it. The close control has a visible label at narrow widths. I inspected opening and closing the dialog by keyboard.

I checked the report's plain-text version using a very long rejection reason. The reason wraps onto an indented continuation line. The next row begins with its identifier at the left margin. A reviewer can follow row boundaries without relying on color.

The final local review index groups parser notes, preview screenshots, and report samples by their artifact names. Each entry describes what its fixture demonstrates. The index avoids a broad completion label and keeps the observations tied to the local material that exists.

events.text: PG-46 irrigation planner must leave the heritage beds on manual watering. Before review, prove no automatic command targets a heritage bed, including after a saved plan is reopened. This is still required if the schedule preview looks correct.

Bed labels. The plan shows bed names, zone numbers, and the suggested start time. Names can wrap and should stay readable beside a long crop description. The heritage marker belongs beside the bed name. A label is useful context for a person inspecting a preview. It does not by itself prevent an automatic watering command. The schedule logic needs to preserve the manual designation when plans are saved and loaded. We have not run that logic check during the label discussion. The sample with the longest bed name showed that the manual label could move onto a third line. I kept the label beside the name and let the crop description wrap below it. This makes the mock easier to inspect. A visible manual label still describes a state rather than enforcing it, so the implementation review needs a separate check of actual command candidates.

Weekly view. The weekly view groups suggested watering windows by day. A narrow display can collapse empty days while leaving a clear date label. The rows should not imply that an omitted day was watered. The local mock plan contains a mix of suggested windows and manual beds. We tried a striped background for manual rows and then used a text label for printing. These presentation decisions do not establish that a reopened saved plan retains manual status. In the narrow weekly mock, a manual-care row remains visible even when there are no suggested windows for its zone. That prevents the preview from suggesting the bed was forgotten. The day headings retain their dates when empty days are collapsed. I inspected the wide and narrow versions using the same local fixture, which makes the layout difference clear without adding evidence about execution.

Soil notes. Soil notes are free text and may mention a bed that shares a zone with another bed. The notes should not be parsed as control commands. A note such as water this bed tomorrow remains a note in this prototype. We need the planner to distinguish display text from its actual schedule data. The local mock includes notes of different lengths to test wrapping. Reading or editing those notes should not activate a controller. A long note includes the words turn on as ordinary prose. The preview renders the words without treating them as a control. This is a useful wording example for the UI review. We should keep notes separate from the structured plan fields when explaining the design. The sample remains a display fixture, so it does not prove anything about commands generated by a reopened plan.

Dry-run legend. The preview legend describes suggested windows, manual care, and unavailable data. A dry run should say clearly that it did not send commands. The word manual should not be replaced by an unexplained icon. The printable view needs the same meaning without color. We compared a shaded row with an outlined row using a local fixture. That comparison concerned legibility. It did not send a schedule or demonstrate controller-side filtering. The draft preview message now says that it generated suggestions. The old wording said that the plan was applied, which could imply execution. I changed the message in the local mock and kept the disabled send control visible. The print view includes the same distinction. A reviewer can now read the report without assuming an irrigation controller was contacted.

Weather panel. The weather panel uses a fixed local forecast fixture. Its purpose here is to show how a rain warning fits beside the proposed plan. The warning may suggest a later start time, but the fixture is not live weather data. The user must still be able to inspect the original suggestion. We kept the panel height stable so the schedule does not jump after loading. No real weather service or irrigation controller was contacted. I compared the page before and after the forecast fixture resolves. The reserved panel height prevents the plan rows from moving under the pointer. The warning includes a fixture label in the local preview notes. If live weather is connected later, that will need its own evidence. This discussion stays within the presentation of the fixed forecast and does not establish any live garden state.

Saved-plan list. The list of saved plans shows a plan name and the time it was saved. A plan name can repeat, so an internal identifier is needed to choose the intended record. The local draft list contains several sample plans with similar names. Opening the wrong sample during a visual review would not show whether the intended saved plan preserves its flags. A proper reopening check must use a known plan and inspect its actual command candidates. The saved-plan list now shows the record identifier in a smaller line under the name. This helps distinguish two local plans with identical names. We can use a known identifier when testing reopen behavior rather than relying on position in the list. The next acceptance check should record that identifier and inspect the resulting command candidates for the heritage and ordinary beds.

Control wording. The preview action is labeled Preview plan. The send action belongs to a later phase and remains disabled in this prototype. Copy should distinguish saving a plan from sending a plan. A saved plan is a stored suggestion, not evidence that the garden was watered. The local fixture lets us test the spacing of those actions. We should avoid a success message that implies execution when only a preview or save occurred. I separated the save confirmation from the send control in the local mock. The save confirmation describes the stored plan and offers a way to return to the plan list. It does not say that watering started. That wording matters because a person may revisit the plan later without this conversation. The implementation must still prove that reopening preserves the manual boundary.

Empty zones. A zone without eligible automatic beds can still show a manual-care note. The preview should not invent an automatic row just to avoid blank space. A zone with missing source data needs a separate message. The sample fixture contains both situations, and we inspected them one at a time. Correct empty-state wording is helpful, but it does not replace the check that heritage-bed commands remain excluded after reopening a saved plan. The unavailable-data state uses a short explanation and keeps the source refresh control visible. The manual-only zone instead shows its manual-care message. I inspected both with local fixtures so the two messages are not accidentally identical. Neither state should create a default automatic command simply to fill the page. The required command check remains open after this layout inspection.

Export notes. The text export includes the plan identifier, generation time, and the list of suggested windows. It should mark manual beds in words. The local export sample wraps long notes under their bed names. We considered omitting manual beds to shorten the report, then kept them so a reviewer can see the boundary of automation. A printed manual label is not proof that command generation obeys the same boundary. That requires inspecting generated commands. The local report now uses a separate manual-care section under the suggested automatic windows. A person can see both groups without interpreting color. The report includes the plan identifier so it can be matched to the saved record. This is useful review material, but the printed grouping cannot prove that the corresponding execution path excludes heritage beds after the saved record is reopened.

Review checklist wording. The checklist should separate visual preview checks from command-generation checks. A checked screenshot item should not automatically check another row. Reopening a saved plan needs its own evidence because serialization can lose a flag even when the first preview is correct. We should record which sample plan was opened and which heritage bed was inspected. The review note can remain concise while preserving this required acceptance step. At this point the conversation is still about how to present the checklist. I left an explicit unchecked line for the reopening test in the review notes. It asks for the chosen plan identifier and the observed command candidates. That keeps the required evidence concrete when someone resumes the work after a layout session. The checklist text itself does not complete the test. A later check must use a known heritage bed and ordinary bed and inspect their generated behavior.
